text: Every device needs an IP address before it can send a single packet, but almost nobody types one in by hand. DHCP is what hands a device an address automatically the moment it joins the network, along with the other settings it needs to actually work.

The whole exchange follows four steps, known as DORA. The new device broadcasts a discover message asking if any DHCP server is out there. A server answers with an offer: a specific address and lease terms. The device broadcasts back a request, formally accepting that offer. And the server sends an acknowledge, confirming the assignment is final.

That address is only borrowed, not permanent. A lease runs for a set period, often a day, and the device quietly renews it before it expires. If a device goes offline and the lease lapses, the address goes back into the pool for someone else. But some devices need the same address every single time — Northbridge Retail's checkout server, for instance — so admins set up a reservation, tying one fixed address to that device's hardware address permanently.

A lease hands over more than just an address. It also includes the subnet mask, the default gateway to reach the rest of the network, which DNS server to use, and how long the lease itself lasts before it needs renewing.
DHCP gets a device onto the network with everything it needs to participate. Up next, lesson twelve: TCP versus UDP, two very different ways that device can actually move data once it has an address.
